A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PARSE and PARSE-10K, and their text, figures, tables, and mathematical content are readable. The supplied v1 ends after the references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Appendices A–D.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, scene-generation comparisons, a 20-participant user study, and statistics for the constructed PARSE-10K dataset.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds analyses of asset composition, scene density, and part-level contacts in its supplement.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2 and 4.1 narrow the documented handling of underspecified relations: v1 describes inferring an asset's lowest part and its surface, whereas v2 describes inferring surfaces within the connected part nodes. The overall PAG, solver, and downstream model procedures remain intact; the appendix's architecture and training details are additional disclosure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same PARSE-10K coverage, COCO real-image examples, three VLM tasks, and scene-generation evaluation. The appendix names the existing 17 room types and characterizes existing assets without establishing additional training or evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, and Qwen3-VL. The scene-generation comparison retains InstructScene and the conditioned and unconditioned variants. Newly cited implementation tools are not added baselines.

E3.justification: The supplementary dataset analyses introduce measurements of object density per square metre, parts per asset, and contacts per scene. Existing MCQ/SGG scoring and the 20-participant, 12-scene user-study design remain unchanged. Appendix D's training configurations and scene-level test separation are newly disclosed settings, not demonstrated revisions to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices B and C.2 add descriptive analyses of category composition, part counts, room types, object density, and contact counts, addressing dataset diversity and interaction complexity. The existing conditioning comparison and grounding-agnostic analysis are retained; no new robustness or sensitivity experiments are reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The new dataset histograms describe composition rather than experimental uncertainty, and the disclosed diffusion noise sampling is a training detail.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical values and rankings. New supplementary findings include an average of 17.4 parts per object, over 55% of scenes exceeding 1.35 objects per square metre, and over 57% containing more than 50 part-level contacts, alongside distributions in Figures 9–13.

T1.justification: Table 4 adds explicit mathematical conditions for spatial relations, including centre-of-mass projection for support, enclosure thresholds, and normal and angle constraints. These extend the formal specification beyond v1's prose descriptions, without adding theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims about PAG, the solver, and improved spatial reasoning and scene generation remain unchanged. The conclusion makes a limited change to the dataset contribution claim: v1 says PARSE-10K was released, whereas v2 says it is constructed, withdrawing the explicit release assertion.

C2.justification: v2 removes the conclusion's specific warning that directional-face contact modeling may deviate on highly oblique contacts, while retaining the manual-construction and canonical-pose limitations. Appendix A.2 additionally describes placement failures caused by empty feasible spaces or exhausted sampling attempts.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D substantially expand reproducibility information: solver pseudocode, surface extraction, asset annotation, simulation and contact extraction, task prompts, scene-disjoint test sets, and detailed model training configurations. Examples include Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct with LoRA rank 8/scaling 32, Sapien's timestep and duration, and diffusion optimization and hardware details. These are disclosures, not evidence of reruns.

R1.justification: v2 adds CAST to related work and six implementation references covering LayerNorm, Graph Transformers, DDPM, LoRA, P3-SAM, and CoACD. The existing references and positioning against object-level scene representations are otherwise retained.

P1.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanatory structure through Appendices A–D, including procedural walkthroughs and task prompts. It also rewrites several PAG and solver passages and captions, edits language, and adds author contact roles and acknowledgments, while preserving the main section order.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 7–14, the spatial-relation dictionary in Table 4, and Algorithm 1. It also revises the overview and PAG/solver diagrams and relocates Figure 5. The existing experimental tables and scene-generation examples retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: v1 refers to supplementary training details absent from the supplied PDF. v2 addresses this important reproducibility gap with solver pseudocode, explicit constraints, asset/contact-processing procedures, and concrete VLM and diffusion training configurations. Its dataset analyses also provide additional evidence for scene complexity. These substantial gains outweigh the loss of the oblique-contact limitation, although that omission reduces transparency. The improvement concerns documentation and assessability; benchmark performance remains unchanged.
